Photograph: Héctor Retamal/AFP/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: No energy ceasefire until Russia stops, Zelenskyy confirms after Trump claim Moscow would need to commit ‘honestly and on a long-term basis’ to peace before Kyiv would de-escalate. What we know on day 1,665 Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Tue 15 Sep 2026 02.15 BST Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 03.18 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukraine will only halt attacks on Russian energy targets if the enemy does likewise and the US guarantees it, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The announcement came after Donald Trump’s uncorroborated claim that both sides have agreed to such a ceasefire. Neither Ukraine nor Russia had said so at time of writing. The US president regularly claims to have brokered what turn out to be nonexistent or extremely shortlived deals between foreign adversaries or with his own overseas enemies, such as Iran. Ukraine’s president said: “So far, no one ‌has seen any genuine ‌willingness on Russia’s part to bring the war to an end. But if our ‌American partners can secure Russia’s genuine readiness to end the war aimed at destroying lives, and to do so honestly and on a long-term basis, Ukraine will take its own de-escalatory steps.” Russia would need to stop attacking Ukraine’s critical infrastructure for its intentions to be taken seriously, Zelenskyy suggested. It comes after Trump tried to blame diesel shortages and high prices on Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries. The main cause is Trump’s own war on Iran – the retaliation for which has crippled the trade in Middle East oil. Russia has banned diesel exports to address dire shortages at home caused by Ukraine’s attacks. But those exports comprise only a fraction of global supply , and the situation most directly affects neighbouring countries such as those in central Asia like Mongolia that rely heavily on supplies from Russian producers. A ⁠Nato fighter jet shot down a drone in Lithuania shortly after ⁠midnight on Tuesday, ⁠the national crisis management centre said. The drone, which likely entered from Belarus , ⁠was shot down near Pratkunai village in southern Lithuania, near Kaunas, the second-largest city, ⁠the centre’s spokesperson said. Its origin was yet ​to be determined at time of writing. A ‌drone alert was issued earlier in the ‌capital, Vilnius, and surrounding region. A ⁠Russian attack on ⁠a farming warehouse killed three people in the ⁠town ​of Pryluky ‌in Ukraine’s ‌northern Chernihiv ‌region, regional police said. Seven ​others were injured. Prosecutors in Germany have charged a German-Ukrainian woman with acting on behalf of Russian intelligence. The woman, identified as Ilona W in line with German privacy rules, is accused of being in contact with an intelligence officer at the Russian embassy in Berlin since at least October 2023. The defendant ran a marketing agency in Berlin and chaired a lobbying group, using these networks to get the intelligence officer into high-profile events, and to try to recruit German defence officials and industry figures. A member of the UK armed forces was killed in a crash in Ukraine on Saturday, Britain’s defence ministry said. It is understood the incident was not a result of hostile action, writes Priya Bharadia . A small number of British personnel in Ukraine provide security to diplomats and support the Ukrainian armed forces. Volodymyr Zelenskyy has formally dismissed Ukraine’s prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, whose office is embroiled in a bribery scandal. Zelenskyy announced the sacking in a government decree. Kravchenko – who has denied the allegations, but resigned on 7 September – posted that he is now outside Ukraine and has started legal action against the head of the national anti-corruption bureau, Nabu, accusing him of “falsifying official documents”. Nabu investigators raided the prosecutor general’s offices and said they had uncovered a network that made payments in return for protecting fraudulent call centres that had “laundered fortunes”. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckge.text: Image source, Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images Image caption, Vitalii Zhykovych appeared in open court during the summer and has spoken to the BBC from prison By Sarah Rainsford ,Â Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent Â and Â Mariana Matveichuk Published 4 hours ago A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was ordered by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency. In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time. Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle". Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent". A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head. But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her. He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut. Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych. Ukrainian agent accused of murdering Monaco bomb suspect changes story Published 9 July For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent. Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev. He understood it was an official mission. "As Reut informed me, this operation [â¦] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says. Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused â he says she was not fully trained â Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead. Image caption, Vladyslav Reut initially confessed but then changed his testimony Reut then communicated directly with Bereszovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives. The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that it is "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies. The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer". Image source, Ukraine prosecutors Image caption, Two screengrabs from a surveillance video captured Anastasia Berezovska just before and during the explosion Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep. It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force. Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack. He called for "the truth, protection, and justice". Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol. She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine. Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting. The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling. Image source, Interpol Image caption, After the Monaco blast, police released an image of Berezovska caught on CCTV The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories. They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine. Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine. Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case. Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us. He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea. "In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison. Image caption, Zhykovych (C) spoke publicly for the first time at a recent custody hearing in Kyiv Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia. But might this story be even murkier? At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present. At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised". "Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court. Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets. When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason. As the investigation continues â into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own. The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son. Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" â meaning Russia. He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation". Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair. Zhykovych says Berezovska called him the day after the Monaco attack, and when he asked why she had done it, she said Reut had promised her a huge fee. "$50,000 doesn't just lie on the streets," she supposedly explained. Residents in her village have told us that Berezovska was saving to buy a flat. But when she travelled to Ukraine to collect the money, she was lured into the woods and shot. Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko and Volodymyr Lozhko. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters View image in fullscreen An image of Pope Leo near the statue of Pope John Paul II outside the Gemelli hospital in Rome. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Pope Leo XIV Pope Leo discharged from hospital after cancer operation Doctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lung Pope Leo lung cancer surgery: what kind of operation did he have and what happens next? Angela Giuffrida in Rome Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.41 EDT Last modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Pope Leo has been discharged from hospital in Rome after undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung . Leo, 71, was deemed “fit for discharge”, his doctors, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement published by the Vatican. He walked unaided from the hospital on Saturday afternoon, to cheers from well-wishers. Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, has been in the Gemelli hospital since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung in order to extract the tumour. “Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge,” the statement said. Doctors said on Wednesday that Leo’s recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They are waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed. Leo was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma. The pontiff celebrated mass in his room on the 10th-floor of the Gemelli hospital in the north-west of the Italian capital before being discharged. View image in fullscreen Leo celebrating Mass at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome. Photograph: Vatican Media/AP The Vatican said he would recite the Angelus prayer on Sunday “from the window of the papal apartment”. It was during his angelus last week, in a rare moment of Vatican transparency, that Leo made the shock announcement to the crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square that a small nodule on his lung had been detected during a check-up. The pope has worked from hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky. The Vatican had originally estimated a week-long stay in hospital. The pope’s appointments had been cancelled until 20 October. It is uncertain if he’ll make an intense 12-day trip to South America planned in November. Cardinal ​Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s secretary of state, told reporters on Friday that Leo may need to readjust his trip schedule, at least with regard to South America, depending on his health. Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome. View image in fullscreen The Gemelli hospital in Rome. Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/AP The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite. https://www.dailysabah.com/opinion/op-ed.text: Opinion Columns Op-Ed Reader's Corner Editorial Ottoman sultan and 'Roman caesar': Mehmed the Conqueror by Ahmet Büyükaksoy Oct 10, 2026 - 12:05 am GMT+3 The monument of Sultan Mehmed II and replicas of the great bronze cannons he ordered to be built for the conquest of Constantinople, in front of Selimiye Mosque, Edirne, Türkiye, Sept. 22, 2018. (Shutterstock Photo) by Ahmet Büyükaksoy Oct 10, 2026 12:05 am Mehmed II was a visionary ruler who united Islamic, Roman and Renaissance traditions to transform the Ottoman Empire and reshape the course of history When one examines Ottoman history, one encounters many illustrious sultans. From Osman Ghazi, the founder of a small principality that would eventually grow into a world empire, to Süleyman the Magnificent, whose achievements left a profound impression on Europe, and Abdülhamid II, who managed to prolong the empire’s existence in the face of mounting internal and external challenges, the Ottoman dynasty produced numerous remarkable rulers. Yet, if you ask me, among all these rulers, Mehmed II occupies a unique place. Few sovereigns in world history transformed both their state and their age as profoundly as he did. Better known as Mehmed the Conqueror, he not only conquered Constantinople and brought an end to the Byzantine Empire, but also laid the foundations of the classical Ottoman state that would dominate three continents for centuries. The reasons for this admiration deserve to be explained. Renaissance man Mehmed II was born in Edirne in 1432. His father, Murad II, an illustrious ruler, initially expected his beloved elder son, şehzade Alaeddin Ali, to succeed him. At the age of 11, Mehmed was sent to Manisa, a traditional training ground for Ottoman princes. There, he received an excellent education under some of the most distinguished scholars of his time. He was also exposed to the ideas of Renaissance humanism, which fostered his lasting interest in classical antiquity and broadened his intellectual horizons beyond the Ottoman world. His studies ranged widely. He read classical histories, learned about Alexander the Great and acquainted himself with European dynastic traditions. Such breadth of learning was unusual for a 15th-century ruler and helped shape the ambitious and intellectually curious sovereign who would later conquer Constantinople. As sultan, Mehmed continued to cultivate this intellectual environment. He patronized scholars, welcomed Greek intellectuals to his court and encouraged the translation of classical works into Turkish. Through these efforts, the cultural and historical legacy of the ancient world became increasingly accessible to the Ottoman elite. A portrait of Sultan Mehmet II, made in 1480 by Venetian artist Gentile Bellini, the collection of the National Gallery, London, U.K. (Getty Images Photo) Mehmed himself amassed an enormous library, reflecting his remarkable intellectual curiosity. His fascination with the classical world and Renaissance culture was perhaps most famously expressed in his commissioning of a portrait from Venetian artist Gentile Bellini, one of the most celebrated Renaissance artists of his time. The resulting portrait is one of the most striking symbols of Mehmed’s unique character: an Ottoman sultan who could appreciate the intellectual traditions of both the Islamic world and Renaissance Europe. Islamic ruler However, Mehmed’s education was not limited to the classical traditions of the ancient and Western worlds. He also received a thorough grounding in Islamic learning under some of the most respected scholars of his age. Equally important was the influence of the renowned Sufi master Akşemseddin, who is traditionally remembered for encouraging the young sultan during the siege of Constantinople and strengthening his resolve to continue the campaign. As a result, Mehmed’s intellectual formation combined the scholarly and spiritual traditions of the Islamic world with a deep appreciation of classical antiquity. It is also worth noting that one of the principal motivations behind Mehmed II’s determination to capture Constantinople was the desire to fulfill a famous prophecy attributed to the Prophet Muhammad. According to a well-known hadith, the prophet declared: “Constantinople shall surely be conquered. What a wonderful commander will its commander be, and what wonderful soldiers will those soldiers be.” For centuries, Muslim rulers had sought to fulfill this prophecy and claim the honor of being the ones destined to realize it. Mehmed was no exception. The conquest of Constantinople therefore represented not only a strategic and political objective, but also a deeply significant religious one. Likewise, Mehmed’s expansionist policies were shaped in part by the ideal of extending the rule and influence of Islam. Like many rulers of his age, he viewed military conquest not merely as a means of increasing his power and prestige, but also as a way of advancing a cause that he regarded as both legitimate and divinely sanctioned. Mehmed also played a crucial role in shaping and organizing the classical structure of the Ottoman state. Islamic law, or Sharia, formed an important foundation of this system, while Mehmed introduced and consolidated institutions that would define the Ottoman political and administrative order for centuries. His reforms and organization provided the foundations of the classical Ottoman state, a structure that remained largely intact until the sweeping reforms of Sultan Mahmud II in the early 19th century. Roman caesar, avenger of Troy After the conquest of Constantinople, Mehmed adopted the title “Caesar of Rome” (Kayser-i Rum), signaling his claim as the legitimate successor to the Roman emperors. This was more than an honorary title. Deeply versed in classical history, Mehmed presented himself as the ruler of a universal empire, thereby challenging the Holy Roman Empire’s claim to embody the Roman imperial tradition. According to the widely recognized eschatological “Four Kingdoms” tradition, the Roman Empire was regarded as the final of the four great earthly kingdoms. As the great Romanian historian Nicolae Iorga famously argued in the early 20th century, the Roman Empire did not simply disappear with the conquest of Constantinople; rather, in a sense, it was transformed into the Ottoman Empire. Whether one accepts Iorga’s interpretation in its entirety or not, Mehmed’s own actions clearly demonstrate that he regarded himself as more than the conqueror of a Byzantine capital. He sought to inherit the political and imperial legacy of Rome. This ambition can also be seen in Mehmed’s fascination with Troy. As historian Erhan Afyoncu has pointed out, when Mehmed visited the Strait of Çanakkale, he visited the ruins of ancient Troy and reportedly searched for the tomb of Hector, the legendary Trojan hero. According to the 15th-century Greek historian Critoboulos, upon finding it, Mehmed declared that Troy had finally been avenged. The story is particularly striking because the Romans themselves were traditionally believed to have descended from the Trojan refugees who escaped the destruction of Troy. In Mehmed’s imagination, therefore, the conquest of Constantinople may have carried a significance that reached far beyond the Byzantine Empire: it connected the Ottoman sultan with the ancient world of Troy, Rome and the universal empire of antiquity. The tomb of the Ottoman Sultan Mehmet the Conqueror, Istanbul, Türkiye, May 5, 2006. (Shuttersock Photo) True intellectual Mehmed II was therefore much more than the conqueror of Constantinople. He was a ruler who stood at the crossroads of several great intellectual and political traditions. He was educated in the Islamic sciences, fascinated by the classical world, surrounded himself with Greek and Italian intellectuals, collected ancient works and brought Renaissance art into his court. At the same time, he was a deeply religious Muslim ruler who saw the conquest of Constantinople as both a political necessity and the fulfillment of a prophecy attributed to the Prophet Muhammad. Yet perhaps what makes Mehmed truly remarkable is that he did not see these traditions as contradictory. For him, the heritage of Greece and Rome, the legacy of Islam and the ambitions of the Ottoman dynasty could be brought together under a single imperial vision. He conquered Constantinople, but he did not simply destroy the Roman world that preceded him. He sought to inherit it. By calling himself Caesar, by collecting the works of classical authors, by engaging with Greek intellectuals and even by associating himself with the ancient story of Troy, Mehmed presented himself as the heir to a much older imperial tradition. This is perhaps why Mehmed II occupies such a unique place in Ottoman history. Osman Ghazi founded the dynasty; Süleyman the Magnificent brought the empire to the height of its power; and Abdülhamid II struggled to preserve it in an age of crisis. Mehmed, however, did something different: he transformed the Ottoman state into an empire with a universal ambition and gave it an intellectual and political identity that would endure for centuries. For me, this is what makes Mehmed the Conqueror so fascinating. He was at once an Ottoman sultan, a Muslim ruler, a patron of Renaissance culture, a student of classical antiquity and, in his own eyes, a Roman caesar. Few rulers in history embodied so many different worlds within a single person. Mehmed II did not merely conquer a city; he claimed its past, reshaped its present and attempted to make himself the architect of its future. In doing so, he became not only the conqueror of Constantinople, but one of the most extraordinary figures of the 15th century.
